{{Lie groups |Semi-simple}}

In the [[mathematical]] field of [[Lie theory]], a '''split Lie algebra''' is a pair <math>(\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{h})</math> where <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is a [[Lie algebra]] and <math>\mathfrak{h} < \mathfrak{g}</math> is a '''splitting [[Cartan subalgebra]]''', where "splitting" means that for all <math>x \in \mathfrak{h}</math>, <math>\operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{g}} x</math> is [[triangularizable]]. If a Lie algebra admits a splitting, it is called a '''splittable Lie algebra'''.<ref>{{Harv |Bourbaki |2005 |loc=Chapter VIII, Section 2: Root System of a Split Semi-Simple Lie Algebra, [https://books.google.com/books?id=Yh1RHnYCDNsC&pg=PA77 p. 77]}}</ref> Note that for reductive Lie algebras, the Cartan subalgebra is required to contain the center.

Over an [[algebraically closed field]] such as the [[complex numbers]], all [[semisimple Lie algebra]]s are splittable (indeed, not only does the Cartan subalgebra act by triangularizable matrices, but even stronger, it acts by diagonalizable ones) and all splittings are conjugate; thus split Lie algebras are of most interest for non-algebraically closed fields.

Split Lie algebras are of interest both because they formalize the [[split real form]] of a complex Lie algebra, and because split semisimple Lie algebras (more generally, split reductive Lie algebras) over any field share many properties with semisimple Lie algebras over algebraically closed fields – having essentially the same representation theory, for instance – the splitting Cartan subalgebra playing the same role as the Cartan subalgebra plays over algebraically closed fields. This is the approach followed in {{Harv|Bourbaki|2005}}, for instance.

== Properties ==
* Over an algebraically closed field, all Cartan subalgebras are conjugate. Over a non-algebraically closed field, not all Cartan subalgebras are conjugate in general; however, in a splittable semisimple Lie algebra all ''splitting'' Cartan algebras are conjugate.
* Over an algebraically closed field, all semisimple Lie algebras are splittable.
* Over a non-algebraically closed field, there exist non-splittable semisimple Lie algebras.<ref>{{Harv|Bourbaki|2005|loc=Chapter VIII, Section 2: Root System of a Split Semi-Simple Lie Algebra, Exercise 2 ''a'' [https://books.google.com/books?id=Yh1RHnYCDNsC&pg=PA77 p. 77]}}</ref>
* In a splittable Lie algebra, there ''may'' exist Cartan subalgebras that are not splitting.<ref>{{Harv|Bourbaki|2005|loc=Chapter VIII, Section 2: Root System of a Split Semi-Simple Lie Algebra, Exercise 2 ''b'' [https://books.google.com/books?id=Yh1RHnYCDNsC&pg=PA77 p. 77]}}</ref>
* Direct sums of splittable Lie algebras and ideals in splittable Lie algebras are splittable.

=== Split real Lie algebras ===
{{see also|Real form}}
For a real Lie algebra, splittable is equivalent to either of these conditions:<ref>{{Harv|Onishchik|Vinberg|1994|loc=p. 157}}</ref>
* The real rank equals the complex rank.
* The [[Satake diagram]] has neither black vertices nor arrows.

Every complex semisimple Lie algebra has a unique (up to isomorphism) split real Lie algebra, which is also semisimple, and is simple if and only if the complex Lie algebra is.<ref>{{Harv|Onishchik|Vinberg|1994|loc=Theorem 4.4, p. 158}}</ref>

For real semisimple Lie algebras, split Lie algebras are opposite to [[compact Lie algebra]]s – the corresponding [[Lie group]] is "as far as possible" from being compact.

== Examples ==
The split real forms for the complex semisimple Lie algebras are:<ref>{{Harv|Onishchik|Vinberg|1994|loc=p. 158}}</ref>
* <math>A_n, \mathfrak{sl}_{n+1}(\mathbf{C}): \mathfrak{sl}_{n+1}(\mathbf{R})</math>
* <math>B_n, \mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbf{C}): \mathfrak{so}_{n,n+1}(\mathbf{R})</math>
* <math>C_n, \mathfrak{sp}_n(\mathbf{C}): \mathfrak{sp}_n(\mathbf{R})</math>
* <math>D_n, \mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbf{C}): \mathfrak{so}_{n,n}(\mathbf{R})</math>
* Exceptional Lie algebras: <math>E_6, E_7, E_8, F_4, G_2</math> have split real forms ''E''I, ''E''V, ''E''VIII, ''F''I, ''G''.
These are the Lie algebras of the split real groups of the complex Lie groups.

Note that for <math>\mathfrak{sl}</math> and <math>\mathfrak{sp}</math>, the real form is the real points of (the Lie algebra of) the same [[algebraic group]], while for <math>\mathfrak{so}</math> one must use the split forms (of maximally indefinite index), as the group SO is compact.
